prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "PROCTER & GAMBLE Co" (ticker PG), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "PG", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: The Procter & Gamble Company
result.industry: Household and personal care consumer products
markets: Home care (Dawn, Fairy, Swiffer, Febreze, Mr. Clean)
Baby, feminine and family care (Pampers, Always, Tampax, Bounty, Charmin)
Beauty: hair care, skin care and personal care (Pantene, Head & Shoulders, Olay, SK-II, Old Spice, Secret)
Health care: oral care and over-the-counter medicines (Crest, Oral-B, Vicks, Metamucil)
Grooming: razors and shavers (Gillette, Venus, Braun)

mission.statement: We will provide branded products and services of superior quality and value that improve the lives of the world’s consumers, now and for generations to come. As a result, consumers will reward us with leadership sales, profit and value creation, allowing our people, our shareholders and the communities in which we live and work to prosper.
mission.source: Company website (us.pg.com, Purpose, Values and Principles)
mission.plain: Make better everyday products that people around the world are happy to buy, so the company, its workers and owners do well too.

about.plain: P&G makes the everyday things people use at home to clean, wash and look after themselves. It sells laundry soap like Tide, dish soap like Dawn, Pampers diapers, Charmin toilet paper, Crest toothpaste and Gillette razors. Its products are sold in about 180 countries. Because people use them up and buy them again every week or month, sales are very steady.
about.customers: Shoppers buy its products through stores and websites such as Walmart (about 16% of P&G's sales), supermarkets, drugstores and Amazon.
about.everyday: If you have washed clothes with Tide, brushed with Crest or Oral-B, or used Bounty paper towels, you have used a P&G product.

money.plain: Tide, Ariel, Downy, Dawn, Swiffer, Febreze
Pantene, Head & Shoulders, Olay, SK-II, Old Spice, Secret
Crest and Oral-B toothpaste and brushes, Vicks, Metamucil
Gillette and Venus razors, Braun shavers

result.summary: Yes. P&G has a wide moat built on trusted category-leading brands (for example over 35% of fabric care and more than 60% of blades and razors in the markets where it competes), unmatched scale in advertising, retail shelf space and supply chain, and steady product innovation. The advantage is durable but not growing fast: in fiscal 2026 net sales rose 3% to $87.0 billion with only 1% organic growth and flat volume, as private label and cost-conscious shoppers press on prices.

pricingPower.evidence: P&G raised prices sharply in fiscal 2022-2023 to offset commodity inflation and kept gross margin above 47%, which recovered to 51.4% in FY2024; in FY2025 pricing added 1 point and volume 1 point, and in FY2026 pricing added 1 point with volume flat, showing that further price rises are now meeting resistance (Baby, Feminine & Family Care price was negative in Q4 FY2026).

moats.evidence: It owns many of the best-known household brands, including Tide, Pampers, Gillette, Crest, Charmin and Dawn, which let it hold about 20% of global hair care, nearly 30% of global oral care and over 30% of global baby care (FY2026 10-K).
Shoppers can switch detergents or diapers at the next store visit at no cost; only habit and trust keep them, plus mild lock-in from Gillette and Oral-B handles and Swiffer refills.
One shopper buying Tide does not make Tide more valuable to another shopper.

With $87.0 billion of FY2026 sales it is the world's biggest advertiser of household goods and gets priority shelf space and supply-chain scale, and it has been named a Gartner Supply Chain 'Master' for 11 consecutive years (2024).
Consumer-goods markets are large and contested by Unilever, Colgate, Kimberly-Clark, Church & Dwight and private label, so there is no natural limit on competitors.
P&G is the incumbent; direct-to-consumer brands such as Dollar Shave Club counter-positioned against it rather than the reverse.
Decades of consumer research, formulation (for example Tide and Dawn upgrades) and low-cost manufacturing know-how are hard to copy, though large rivals like Unilever have similar skills.
It holds patents on product technologies and a famed promote-from-within management bench, but no exclusive asset rivals cannot reach.

customers.evidence: Shoppers keep repurchasing leading brands such as Tide, Pampers, Charmin and Dawn week after week, and P&G sells in about 180 countries; loyalty is strongest in the US, while share pressure from private label and local rivals is greater in some international markets such as China.

talent.evidence: P&G is known as a 'CEO factory' for marketers and ranked #19 on Fortune's 2026 World's Most Admired Companies list, #1 in packaged goods on Forbes' 2025 America's Best Employers for Company Culture and #19 on Forbes' 2025 Best Employers for Women; it promotes almost entirely from within.

product.evidence: Many of its brands are category leaders (Tide in US laundry, Gillette in razors with over 60% share, Oral-B in electric toothbrushes) and it was named on Fortune's 2026 America's Most Innovative Companies list, though rivals and store brands often match performance at lower prices.

competitors.name: Unilever
competitors.note: Global rival in hair care (Dove, Sunsilk), skin care, deodorants (Rexona, Axe), and home care (Persil/Omo, Cif) in many emerging markets.

competitors.name: Colgate-Palmolive
competitors.note: Global oral care leader competing with Crest and Oral-B; also dish soap (Palmolive) and personal care.

competitors.name: Kimberly-Clark
competitors.note: Huggies diapers vs Pampers, Kotex vs Always, Kleenex and Scott vs Puffs, Bounty and Charmin; agreed in November 2025 to acquire Kenvue.

competitors.name: Church & Dwight
competitors.note: Arm & Hammer laundry detergent, OxiClean and Batiste dry shampoo in the US.

competitors.name: The Clorox Company
competitors.note: Home cleaning, Glad bags and Pine-Sol vs Mr. Clean and Swiffer in the US.

competitors.name: Kenvue
competitors.note: Listerine vs Crest mouthwash, Neutrogena vs Olay, Tylenol and Zyrtec vs P&G OTC; being acquired by Kimberly-Clark.

competitors.name: Haleon
competitors.note: Sensodyne and Parodontax toothpaste vs Crest, and cold and flu remedies vs Vicks.

competitors.name: L'Oréal
competitors.note: Hair care (Elvive, Garnier) and skin care vs Pantene, Olay and SK-II; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: Reckitt Benckiser
competitors.note: Finish dishwasher detergent, Lysol, Vanish and Durex; competes in home care and health; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: Henkel
competitors.note: Persil and all laundry detergents and Schwarzkopf hair care, especially in Europe; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: The Estée Lauder Companies
competitors.note: Prestige skin care vs SK-II and Olay's premium lines, especially in Asian travel retail.

competitors.name: Edgewell Personal Care
competitors.note: Schick and Billie razors vs Gillette and Venus.

competitors.name: Essity
competitors.note: Tena incontinence, Libero diapers and Tork/Lotus tissue, mainly in Europe and Latin America; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: Private label (Walmart Great Value, Costco Kirkland, Amazon Basics and others)
competitors.note: Cheaper store brands in diapers, paper towels, detergent and razors are the biggest pressure on P&G pricing.

estimates.name: Private label (Walmart Great Value, Costco Kirkland, Amazon Basics and others)

threats: Private label and cheaper store brands gaining as cost-pressured shoppers trade down, shown by flat FY2026 volume and only 1% organic growth
Higher raw material, energy and transport costs: P&G expects a roughly $1 billion after-tax commodity headwind in fiscal 2027
Retailer concentration: Walmart is about 16% of sales and the top ten customers about 43%, giving big retailers bargaining power
Weakness in China and other international markets, including local challengers in diapers and skin care (SK-II)
Consolidation of rivals, such as Kimberly-Clark's agreed acquisition of Kenvue, creating a larger competitor in health and personal care
Shift of shopping to e-commerce and direct-to-consumer brands, which weakens the advantage of physical shelf space

ceo.name: Shailesh Jejurikar
ceo.background: Career P&G executive since 1989 (fabric care, then chief operating officer from 2021); BA from Mumbai University and MBA from IIM Lucknow

c1.evidence: P&G leads household and personal care, a mature industry where its own organic sales grew only 1% in fiscal 2026.

c2.evidence: Shoppers choose trusted, better-performing brands like Tide, Pampers and Gillette, backed by heavy advertising, research and shelf presence that rivals have struggled to copy for decades, though cheaper private label is a steady threat.

c3.evidence: Its brands (Tide, Pampers, Gillette, Crest, Charmin) are household names and P&G is the default leader in consumer packaged goods, even if many shoppers know the brands better than the P&G name.

c4.evidence: Its long-standing purpose to 'improve the lives of the world's consumers' is repeated often, but it openly ties it to 'leadership sales, profit and value creation', so it is a well-run commercial mission rather than a world-changing one.

c6.evidence: “trusted, everyday, Tide and Pampers, big consumer giant” — the impression is mostly positive, with some criticism over price rises and ingredient or packaging concerns.

c7.evidence: Household and personal care is a very large market but grows slowly, roughly with population and incomes, rather than riding a fast secular trend.

c8.evidence: It can push existing brands into emerging markets and premium tiers and expand adult incontinence (Always Discreet) and health care, but it is shrinking its portfolio under its 2025 restructuring rather than entering big new markets.

m1.evidence: Jejurikar has a clear consumer-first 'superiority' strategy, citing innovations like upgraded Tide formulas, but he is a steady operator rather than a visionary.

m2.evidence: He is a career P&G employee since 1989 who became CEO on January 1, 2026, not a founder.

m4.evidence: He emphasises serving consumers and P&G's promote-from-within culture, but there is little public evidence of a distinctive servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: P&G's innovation and brand-building culture is decades old; Jejurikar is continuing it rather than having built it.

m6.evidence: He is deeply involved in product and brand decisions from his fabric care years (Tide, Ariel, Downy), but has a business (BA and MBA) background, not an engineering one.

m7.evidence: There is no public controversy, but too little is known yet about his personal character and priorities beyond P&G's stated purpose and values.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Jejurikar at a top university has been reported.

m8b.evidence: He keeps a low public profile typical of P&G executives.

m9.evidence: As COO from 2021 he helped deliver steady growth (sales rose from $76.1 billion in FY2021 to $87.0 billion in FY2026), but his first months as CEO saw flat volume, falling operating income and a 15% drop in Q4 FY2026 diluted EPS.

m10.evidence: P&G runs ongoing productivity programs, including a 2025 restructuring costing $1.0-$1.6 billion that cut employees about 4% to roughly 104,000 in FY2026, but it is not known for Bezos-style frugality.

c10.evidence: Billions of people use its diapers, detergents, toothpaste and period products, which improve hygiene and daily life, though these are useful conveniences more than life-changing technology.

p2.evidence: Its products matter for hygiene and are hard to make at scale, but making detergent or razors is not extremely hard for well-funded rivals and store brands.

f1.evidence: Net sales rose every year from $76,118 million in FY2021 to $80,187M, $82,006M, $84,039M, $84,284M and $87,032M in FY2026.

f2.evidence: Gross margin slipped from 51.2% in FY2021 to 50.2% in FY2026 and operating margin from 23.6% to 22.7%, after dipping to about 47% gross margin in FY2022-23.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 total debt of $34,138 million was well above cash of $9,942 million but under two years of operating cash flow ($19,556 million in FY2026), and shareholders' equity was positive at $54,311 million.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $17,986 million in FY2021 to $19,748 million in FY2026 and operating cash flow from $18,371 million to $19,556 million, but both fell in some years (operating income dropped 3% in FY2026).

v1.evidence: Tide, Dawn and Gillette are often rated top performers and are the default choice for many shoppers, but cheaper rivals and store brands are good enough for many people, so it is not a clear-cut choice like NVIDIA.

v2.evidence: P&G ranked #19 on Fortune's 2026 World's Most Admired Companies, #1 in packaged goods on Forbes' 2025 America's Best Employers for Company Culture and #19 on Forbes' 2025 Best Employers for Women, and is famous for training future CEOs.

c5.evidence: Families worldwide would miss familiar brands like Pampers, Tide and Always for a while, but Unilever, Kimberly-Clark, Colgate and store brands would quickly fill most of the gap.
